Seminar Title:

Rational Design of Advanced Electrode Materials for High-Energy and Wide-Temperature Sodium-Ion Batteries

Seminar Type:

Contact:

Prof. Ajit Behera PIC, Seminar; MM Dept. E mail: beheraajit@nitrkl.ac.in

Abstract:

The global transition toward carbon-neutral energy systems demands rechargeable batteries that combine high performance with elemental abundance and long-term sustainability. Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have emerged as one of the most promising alternatives to lithium-ion technology because of the widespread availability and low cost of sodium. However, their practical deployment remains hindered by sluggish Na-ion transport, limited electronic conductivity, interfacial degradation, poor low-temperature kinetics, and inadequate cycling stability of existing electrode materials. Addressing these challenges requires simultaneous optimization of both cathode and anode chemistries together with a mechanistic understanding of sodium-storage processes. This work presents an integrated materials-design strategy that combines transition-metal substitution, heteroatom engineering, carbon modification, advanced characterization, and first-principles modelling to develop high-performance sodium-ion battery electrodes with enhanced electrochemical stability over a broad operating temperature range. A rational dual-doping strategy was employed to engineer NASICON-type Na₃V₂(PO₄)₂F₃ (NVPF) cathodes through controlled Fe–Cr and Fe–Ni substitution using a scalable rota-tumbler-assisted sol–gel synthesis approach. Simultaneous cationic substitution modifies the local electronic structure, optimizes Na-ion diffusion pathways, suppresses polarization, and improves charge-transfer kinetics while reducing dependence on vanadium. The optimized Fe–Cr substituted composition, Na₃V₁.₉Fe₀.₀₉₅Cr₀.₀₀₅(PO₄)₂F₃, delivers a reversible discharge capacity of 119.85 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 C, together with excellent rate capability and prolonged cycling stability. More importantly, Fe–Ni dual substitution produces a highly robust cathode that maintains outstanding electrochemical performance across an exceptionally wide temperature window spanning −21.1 °C to 55 °C, highlighting the effectiveness of compositional engineering in overcoming kinetic limitations under both sub-zero and elevated-temperature conditions. Comprehensive electrochemical analyses, impedance spectroscopy, and post-cycling structural investigations reveal reduced interfacial resistance, accelerated sodium diffusion, and enhanced structural integrity as the primary origins of the improved performance. To complement the optimized cathode, a boron–phosphorus dual-doped hard carbon anode was developed through simultaneous heteroatom and defect engineering. The synergistic incorporation of boron and phosphorus enlarges the interlayer spacing, increases the concentration of electrochemically active defects, improves electronic conductivity, and generates additional sodium-storage sites. Consequently, the engineered hard carbon exhibits enhanced reversible capacity, improved initial coulombic efficiency, superior rate capability, and outstanding long-term cycling stability compared with conventional hard carbon. Density Functional Theory calculations demonstrate that dual heteroatom incorporation lowers the electronic band gap, strengthens sodium adsorption, facilitates charge transport, and minimizes structural expansion during sodiation, providing a robust theoretical framework that directly supports the experimental observations. The optimized cathode and anode were subsequently integrated into a full sodium-ion cell, which demonstrates excellent electrochemical compatibility, high coulombic efficiency, durable cycling behaviour, and reliable operation under a wide range of temperatures. Beyond improving individual electrode performance, this work establishes a comprehensive design paradigm that links crystal chemistry, defect engineering, electronic structure modulation, and electrode–electrolyte interfacial stability to battery performance. Collectively, these findings provide new mechanistic insights into sodium-storage behaviour and demonstrate that coordinated engineering of both electrodes can substantially overcome the intrinsic limitations of current sodium-ion batteries. The materials-design principles established in this work offer a scalable pathway toward the development of high-energy-density, temperature-resilient, and commercially viable sodium-ion batteries for large-scale stationary energy storage and next-generation electric transportation.
